intro.html: Between “I know” and “I have no idea” lies a lot of ground, and careful thinkers have words for every step of it. You can presume without proof, speculate with no evidence at all, find a claim plausible or dubious, hold a conviction firmly, or stay skeptical until you see the facts. These words fill the science and history passages of every reading test.

Believing: conviction (a firm belief), tenet (a principle a group holds), presume (take as true without proof), dogmatic (sure, and closed to evidence). Weighing: plausible (seems likely), speculate (guess without evidence). Doubting: skeptical (wants proof), dubious (doubtful, or shady), cynical (distrusts people’s motives), fallacy (a mistaken belief or bad reasoning).

words.ex: Dad was {skeptical} when the ad promised a car that would never need a single repair.
words.ctx: The salesman swore the vacuum could clean a whole house in five minutes, but Nana remained {skeptical} and asked to see it work on her own carpet first.
words.etym: From Greek skeptikos, “inquiring,” from skeptesthai, “to look at, to examine.”

mn.text: Rex claims his round rock is a dinosaur egg, so Ada pulls out her magnifying glass and looks very closely before believing a word. She is {skeptical}.

scene.alt: A scientist examines a so-called dinosaur egg through a magnifying glass before believing it.

words.ex: Ivy was {dubious} about her brother’s promise to clean the kitchen by himself.
words.ctx: The deal sounded too good to be true, and it came from a company with a {dubious} record: three of its last four products had been recalled.
words.note: Dubious can describe a doubting person (“I’m dubious”) or a thing that deserves doubt (“a dubious claim”).

mn.text: A sign promises shoes that let you fly for five dollars. Grandpa Gus squints at it, full of doubt, and the seller looks shady too. Gus is {dubious}.

scene.alt: A grandfather squints doubtfully at a shady seller offering “flying shoes.”

words.ex: Zoe’s excuse was {plausible}: the bus really had broken down that morning.
words.ctx: The detective’s theory was {plausible}, since it explained both the muddy boots and the open window, but she still needed proof before she could be sure.
words.etym: From Latin plausibilis, “deserving applause,” from plaudere, “to applaud.”

mn.text: Zoe says she is late because the bus broke down, and there it sits, steaming at the corner. Her excuse earns a nod and a clap: it is {plausible}.

scene.alt: A girl points to a broken-down, smoking bus as her excuse, and her teacher accepts it.

words.def: a firmly held belief; also, a finding of guilt in court
words.ex: Nell spoke with {conviction} about saving the old oak trees.
words.ctx: Though everyone laughed at her plan, Tia held to her {conviction} that the empty lot could become a garden, and by summer it was full of tomatoes.
words.etym: From Latin convictio, from convincere, “to overcome, to prove”: con (thoroughly) + vincere (to conquer).
words.note: In a courtroom, a conviction is a finding of guilt: “The conviction was overturned on appeal.”

mn.cue: con-VICT-ion: a belief that WINS you
mn.text: Everyone laughs at Tia’s plan to turn the empty lot into a garden, but she plants her flag and won’t budge. She speaks with {conviction}.

scene.alt: A determined woman plants a flag in an empty lot she believes will become a garden.

words.def: a principle or belief held as true by a group
words.ex: A basic {tenet} of the hiking club is to leave no trash behind.
words.ctx: Fair play was the central {tenet} of the soccer league: every child got equal time on the field, no matter the score.
words.etym: From Latin tenet, “he holds,” from tenere, “to hold”: a tenet is a belief a group holds.
words.note: A tenet (a principle) is not a tenant (someone who rents a home).

mn.cue: TEN = HOLD: a belief the club HOLDS
mn.text: The hiking club’s sign lists the beliefs its members hold to, and number one is “Leave no trash.” Each rule they hold is a {tenet}.

scene.alt: Two hikers carry out their trash beside a club sign whose first rule is leave no trash.

words.def: insisting one’s opinions are true without considering evidence
words.ex: Our {dogmatic} neighbor insists there is only one right way to mow a lawn.
words.ctx: Good scientists change their minds when new evidence appears, but the {dogmatic} professor refused even to look at the results that contradicted his theory.
words.etym: From Greek dogma, “opinion, belief,” from dokein, “to seem, to think.”

mn.cue: DOG + MAT: a dog that won’t budge
mn.text: Rufus has decided that the doormat is his, and no treat, toy or argument will move him an inch. Stuck to an opinion like a dog on its mat is {dogmatic}.

scene.alt: A stubborn dog refuses to leave its mat even when a boy offers a bone.

words.def: to suppose something is true without proof
words.ex: I {presume} you’ve already eaten, since there are crumbs on your shirt.
words.ctx: Seeing the wet umbrellas by the door, Dad {presumed} it was raining, but he stepped outside into bright sunshine; the umbrellas had only been left there to dry.
words.etym: From Latin praesumere, “to take beforehand”: prae (before) + sumere (to take).

mn.cue: PRE-SUME: take it as true BEFORE checking
mn.text: Omar sees wet umbrellas by the door and pops his own open before stepping out, into blazing sunshine. He did not check; he chose to {presume}.

scene.alt: A man holds an open umbrella under a bright, cloudless sun, looking puzzled.

words.def: to form ideas or theories without firm evidence
words.ex: Fans {speculated} about who would win the baking contest.
words.ctx: With no letters or diaries to go on, historians can only {speculate} about why the village was abandoned: perhaps a flood, perhaps a sickness, perhaps a better harvest elsewhere.
words.etym: From Latin speculari, “to watch, to look out,” from specere, “to look.”

mn.cue: SPEC-ulate: look and guess, no peeking
mn.text: The kids stare at the big wrapped box and guess: a bike? a puppy? a robot? With no way to peek inside, all they can do is {speculate}.

scene.alt: Two children stare at a big wrapped present, guessing what is inside.

words.def: a mistaken belief, or a flaw in reasoning
words.ex: “Everyone I know likes pizza, so everyone in the world must like pizza” is a {fallacy}.
words.ctx: His argument rested on a {fallacy}: just because the rooster crows before sunrise does not mean that the rooster makes the sun come up.
words.etym: From Latin fallacia, “deceit,” from fallere, “to deceive,” the root of false.

mn.text: The rooster crows, the sun comes up, and he proudly believes his crowing made it rise. That reasoning falls apart: it is a {fallacy}.

scene.alt: A proud rooster crows and claims credit for the rising sun.

words.def: believing that people act only out of self-interest
words.ex: The {cynical} shopper assumed the free samples must be some kind of trick.
words.ctx: When the new neighbor offered to help paint his fence, Victor was {cynical}: he assumed she must want something in return, though she only wanted to be friendly.
words.etym: From Greek kynikos, “doglike,” the name given to the Cynics, ancient Greek thinkers who scorned wealth, comfort and custom.

mn.text: Nell brings her new neighbor a pie, and Victor squints: “What’s the catch? What do you want?” He thinks every kindness hides a selfish reason. Victor is {cynical}.

scene.alt: A friendly woman offers a pie, and a suspicious man wonders what she really wants.

head: doubting word
what it doubts
rows: either; or the thing itself is shady
after.cap: A skeptic doubts what people say; a cynic doubts why they say it.

after.html: tenet (a principle) and tenant (a renter) sound alike but differ: both come from ten, hold. A tenet is a belief a group holds; a tenant holds a lease. And to presume is to take something as true before checking (pre-), while to speculate is to guess with no real evidence at all.

items.q: Victor thinks his neighbor only helped him so she could borrow his ladder. Victor is being…
items.why: Assuming that people act only out of self-interest is cynical. Skeptical means doubting claims and wanting evidence.

items.q: Which sentence uses the right word?
choices: Honesty is a central tenet of the club.
The tenet of the apartment paid her rent.
The tenet moved into the upstairs flat.
items.why: A tenet is a principle. A person who rents is a tenant.

items.q: True or false: a plausible explanation is one that seems reasonable.
items.why: True. Plausible means seeming reasonable or likely, though not yet proven.

choices: a coach who refuses to try any play but his own, no matter what the results show
a scientist who changes her theory when new data arrive
a student who asks many questions before deciding
items.why: Dogmatic means insisting your opinions are right without considering evidence.
